items.question: What happens in cognition when the word for pot is heard?
premises: When the word for pot is heard, a cognition of broad base, belly, and so on arises.
In that cognition, convention, memory, and similar factors are present.
These factors are of the same kind as in other acts of recognition.
items.inference: Hearing a word produces a complex cognition involving remembered conventions and associated features.
items.plain_english: When the word 'pot' is heard, a cognition arises of its broad base, belly, and other features; in that cognition, convention, memory, and similar factors are present in the same way.

items.question: How does clear awareness arise in the examination of a gem?
premises: In the examination of a gem, one awakens one's own awareness.
This awakening occurs through assemblages of other cognitions.
The resulting awareness stands forth as clear in nature.
items.inference: Clear awareness of an object is brought about through the support of other cognitions.
items.plain_english: Just as in examining a gem one awakens one's own clear awareness through assemblages of other cognitions, so that awareness stands forth distinctly.

items.question: What role do other cognitions play once the gem's reality shines forth?
premises: The reality of the gem shines forth from the connection with the final awakened clear awareness.
At that point, other cognitions have no further use.
The decisive illumination comes from that final awareness itself.
items.inference: Once the final clear awareness arises, auxiliary cognitions are no longer operative.
items.plain_english: Then, through the connection with the final awakened clear awareness, the reality of the gem shines forth; at that point the other cognitions have no further use.

rows.grounds: demonstrative pronoun referring to other cognitions
tasya + eva + avabhāsa + yoge, locative compound

items.question: Why do auxiliary cognitions lose their usefulness at the moment of manifestation?
premises: Those other cognitions served only as causes for awakening that final awareness.
In the very connection of that awareness's manifestation, they have no usefulness.
Their role is preparatory rather than constitutive of the final illumination.
items.inference: Auxiliary cognitions are instrumental causes but not operative in the final manifestation itself.
items.plain_english: Those other cognitions exercised causality only for awakening that awareness; for in the very connection of its manifestation, they have no usefulness.

items.question: Does verbal cognition also involve a single clear illumination like the gem example?
premises: The example of a child and a gem-cutter's knowledge shows a single clear cognition.
This example applies by itself to verbal cognition as well.
In verbal cognition too, one clear illumination-cognition arises.
items.inference: Verbal cognition, like perceptual expertise, culminates in a single clear illuminating awareness.
uncertainties: vaikaṭika is read as gem-cutter or lapidary; context supports that sense.
items.plain_english: From such an example as the knowledge of a child and a gem-cutter, in verbal cognition too there is indeed by itself one clear cognition of illumination.

items.question: What is the nature of the cognition that arises immediately after hearing a word?
premises: When such a word is heard, a cognition arises immediately after.
That cognition occurs in the manifestation of meaning.
It is a determinate cognition of a specific extent and character.
items.inference: The immediate post-hearing cognition is a determinate manifestation of meaning.
items.plain_english: Therefore, when such a word is heard, whatever cognition arises immediately after in the manifestation of meaning, that cognition is of this extent and of such a character.

rows.grounds: objection particle, sandhi form of nanu

items.question: Can the unity of a pot serve as an analogy for the relation between word and meaning?
premises: The meaning stands there with that extent, like the prior and posterior parts of a pot.
An objector suggests the pot may be one whole composed of parts.
This raises the question whether word and meaning share a similar unity.
items.inference: The analogy of a unified whole is introduced to probe the relation between word and meaning.
items.plain_english: That meaning, of that extent, stands there like the prior and posterior parts of a pot. But surely that pot may be one whole composed of parts?

items.question: Why is the analogy between a pot's unity and word-meaning unity rejected?
premises: The objector claims there is no unity between word and meaning.
Therefore the objector questions how such sameness could hold.
This objection arises from eyes clouded by the habit of grasping difference.
items.inference: The denial of word-meaning unity is attributed to a habitual perception of difference.
items.plain_english: But there is no unity of word and meaning, so how could there be such sameness? Alas, one whose eyes are clouded by the darkness of habitual grasping of difference!

items.question: What does the undivided Bhairava assume within himself despite the objector's clouded vision?
premises: Even with the application of the collyrium of true reasoning, the objector has not attained clear vision.
The undivided Lord Bhairava assumes the state of both enjoyed and enjoyer.
This assumption occurs within Bhairava himself.
items.inference: The ultimate nondual reality encompasses both subject and object within itself.
items.plain_english: Even with the application of the collyrium of true reasoning, he has not attained clear vision. This undivided Lord Bhairava assumes within himself the state of both the enjoyed and the enjoyer.

items.question: What happens to the earlier objection once Bhairava's nondual fullness is established?
premises: Bhairava, always full-bodied, unifies everything within himself.
This nondual fullness has been established previously.
Given that establishment, the earlier question loses its basis.
items.inference: Once nondual fullness is established, the objection about word-meaning separation cannot arise.
items.plain_english: Having unified everything within himself, always full-bodied — when this has been established previously, what possibility remains for this question?

items.question: Does the primacy of perceptual awareness extend beyond ordinary perception to other means of knowing?
premises: The argument extends to comparison and other means of knowing.
In all these cases, what appears is clearly of the form of awareness-perception.
This perceptual form of awareness shines forth everywhere.
items.inference: All valid means of knowing ultimately manifest as forms of perceptual awareness.
items.plain_english: Therefore, thus, in comparison and in other means of knowing as well, it is clearly the form of awareness-perception alone that appears everywhere.

items.question: How does a blind person experience clear cognition without visual perception?
premises: Even a blind person perceives each respective form through touch, sound, and other senses.
That person cognizes a clarity of such a kind.
The clarity is genuine even without visual input.
items.inference: Clear perceptual awareness does not depend exclusively on vision but arises through available modes of cognition.
items.plain_english: Even a blind person, perceiving each respective form through touch, sound, and so on, cognizes that clarity of just such a kind.

items.question: Do those congenitally deaf also attain clear cognition of things?
premises: Those congenitally deaf apprehend aspects of things through form, touch, and other senses.
They apprehend these aspects clearly.
For them, cognition is never entirely unknown in any respect.
items.inference: Clear cognition of objects is available through non-auditory senses as well.
uncertainties: jātijaḍā is read as congenitally deaf or congenitally dull; the sensory examples favor deaf.
items.plain_english: Thus those congenitally deaf apprehend an aspect of things clearly through form, touch, and so on; for them cognition is never unknown anywhere.

items.question: Can a congenitally blind person form a vivid appreciative cognition of beauty?
premises: A congenitally blind person touches a woman's limbs.
From that touch he forms an appreciative cognition expressed as a lake of beauty and a shoot of the garden of youth.
He is pleased by that cognition.
items.inference: Vivid and affectively charged cognition can arise through non-visual sensory experience.
items.plain_english: Saying 'this is a lake of beauty, a shoot in the garden of youth,' a congenitally blind person is pleased from touching her limbs.

items.question: How can a deaf person appreciate a song as ornamented?
premises: A deaf person sees the singer's face.
From that visual perception alone, he concludes that the singing is ornamented.
He is satisfied by that cognition.
items.inference: Aesthetic appreciation can arise from cross-modal cues even when the primary sense is absent.
items.plain_english: Saying 'ah, he sings with ornament,' a deaf person, merely by seeing the singer's face, is satisfied by that alone.

items.question: What follows from establishing perception as the sole unrivaled means of knowing?
premises: Perception alone expands without rival.
This has been shown through the preceding examples.
Therefore a brief consideration of its fruit is now begun.
items.inference: Having established perception's supremacy, the discussion turns to its practical result.
items.plain_english: Thus perception alone expands without rival; therefore a brief consideration of its fruit and so on is now begun.

items.question: Is talk of difference compatible with the true fruit of cognition?
premises: Cognition itself is essentially reflective awareness.
The fruit of cognition must accord with that essential nature.
Talk of difference does not fit that fruit.
items.inference: Because cognition is reflective awareness, difference-based accounts are not suited to its fruit.
items.plain_english: That very cognition is surely of the nature of the essence of reflective awareness; therefore talk of difference is not at all well suited with regard to its fruit.

items.question: What is the ultimate fruit if practical cognitions like avoidance are considered?
premises: One might propose avoidance and similar cognitions as the fruit.
Even those arise from manifestation.
Alternatively, ultimate awareness is self-luminous.
items.inference: Even practical fruits depend on manifestation, pointing back to self-luminous awareness as ultimate.
items.plain_english: Let avoidance and similar cognitions be the fruit; yet even that comes from manifestation. Or else, awareness is self-luminous and ultimate.

items.question: What is the final and primary fruit recognized everywhere in this system?
premises: That self-luminous awareness is the final fruit everywhere.
This is well determined.
Joy and similar experiences, spoken of as primary fruits, are included within it.
items.inference: The ultimate fruit is self-luminous awareness, within which joy and other fruits are subsumed.
items.plain_english: That indeed is the final fruit, well determined everywhere; joy and so on, which is spoken of everywhere here as the primary fruit, is included in it.

items.question: Where does the primary fruit of joy ultimately come to rest?
premises: Joy and similar fruits come to rest in one's own awareness.
That awareness is the full self.
Thus perception expands on all sides as this awareness.
items.inference: All experiential fruits culminate in repose within the full self-awareness, which is perception itself.
items.plain_english: It comes to rest in that own awareness, in the full self. Therefore, thus, this perception fully expands on all sides.

items.question: What accomplishments arise for one devoted to the practice of this perception?
premises: One may be devoted to the practice of this perception.
Such devotion leads to accomplishments.
These include hearing from afar, inclined toward what is spoken by Brahma and others, beginning from kala and so on.
items.inference: Practice of this perception yields extraordinary accomplishments, including distant hearing.
uncertainties: The compound brahmādibhāṣitaśrautapraunmukhyena is dense; the sense is an inclination toward hearing what is spoken by Brahma and others.
items.plain_english: For one devoted to the practice of this, what accomplishment does not arise? Beginning from kala and so on, through an inclination toward hearing what is spoken by Brahma and others...

rows.grounds: ablative adverb, sandhi form of dūrāt

items.question: What specific powers arise from devotion to this perceptual practice?
premises: Hearing-cognition from afar arises quickly.
Even in an aspect of a thing seen only by the mind, clear cognition arises.
These arise abundantly through the practice.
items.inference: The practice produces both distant sensory cognition and clear mental cognition.
items.plain_english: Hearing-cognition from afar quickly arises; even in an aspect of a thing seen by the mind, the arising of clear cognition indeed occurs abundantly.

items.question: Why is the arising of clear cognition unsurprising when overcome by the power of self-reflection?
premises: When something is overcome by the power of one's own reflective awareness, extraordinary cognition can arise.
Such arising is not surprising.
The Spanda scripture states this for an attentive mind.
items.inference: The power of self-reflection naturally produces heightened cognition, as confirmed by the Spanda tradition.
items.plain_english: What wonder is it if this arises when overcome by the power of one's own reflective awareness? So it is said in the Spanda scripture, even in an attentive mind.

items.question: How does the discussion conclude regarding perception and the universe of the supreme lord?
premises: The Spanda scripture says that in an attentive mind it shines forth ever more clearly.
Further elaboration is unnecessary.
In this way, this entire universe is indeed perception belonging to the supreme lord.
items.inference: The universe is nothing other than the supreme lord's perception, shining with increasing clarity.
items.plain_english: It shines forth ever more clearly — enough of much elaboration. In this way, this entire universe is indeed the perception of the supreme lord.
